\section[serio]{serio — serious}

\label{lesson:IT-C127-serio}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Italian for bad; nasty, then the Italian for kind.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: serio}
\textbf{serio} — \textquotedblleft{}serious\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{serio} $\leftarrow$ Latin \emph{serius}, \textquotedblleft{}earnest, grave\textquotedblright{} — a learned borrowing, taken from written Latin. (EtymDB 2.1 records the Latin word.)
\end{cousinweb}

\section[sbagliato]{sbagliato — wrong}

\label{lesson:IT-C127-sbagliato}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Italian for serious, then the Italian for right.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: sbagliato}
\textbf{sbagliato} — \textquotedblleft{}wrong\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{sbagliato} is the past participle of the verb for \textquotedblleft{}to make a mistake\textquotedblright{}, which comes from \emph{abbagliare}, \textquotedblleft{}to dazzle\textquotedblright{}, with \emph{s-} in place of \emph{a-}. EtymDB 2.1 takes that verb apart as \emph{s-} plus an old verb \emph{bagliare}; only where \emph{bagliare} came from is uncertain.
\end{cousinweb}
